name: LoreTypes
tagline: A typing trainer that drills you on passages of fiction and game lore instead of random word lists.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: A typing trainer is one of the most solved problems in frontend engineering: a text buffer, a keypress handler, a WPM formula, and a chart. An agent can build the whole loop in a single session, no backend, no accounts, everything in localStorage. The only genuinely hard part is the text itself, and that is a sourcing problem rather than a coding problem: public domain fiction is free, modern game and novel lore is not yours to bundle. What you give up is curation, the feel of a well tuned input loop, and someone else's taste in passages. If you already have text you want to type, the DIY version is better than fine.
coreLoopDIY: Loads a passage from your own text packs, scores keystrokes live with per-character highlighting, and stores WPM and accuracy history locally so you can watch yourself improve.
requirements: Your own passage files, public domain or self-written
whatYouLose: A curated passage library someone else sourced and formatted
Whatever licensed or original lore the paid product ships
Tuned input feel: caret behavior, error handling, backspace rules take iteration
Cross-device history without you wiring sync
moatNotes: The engine is trivial. The passages are the product, and the good ones are either licensed, original, or hand curated.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because nobody who wants typing practice wants a side project first. The paid version has passages already chosen, chunked to sane lengths, and free of the formatting junk that ruins a drill, plus an input loop that has been sanded down by real users complaining about caret lag and backspace behavior. A one-shot build nails the mechanics and then sits there empty, waiting for you to go find text.
notes: The typing engine is an afternoon; building a passage library you actually enjoy typing is the part that never ends.
prompt:
Build a local-first typing practice app. Empty folder, no backend, no accounts, no telemetry.

Stack: Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind. State in React, persistence in localStorage. No server, no database, no auth, no analytics. Deploys as static files.

Content model:
- A /content folder with JSON "packs": { id, title, source, passages: [{ id, title, text }] }.
- Ship three example packs using public domain text only (Jules Verne, Mary Shelley, Norse mythology translations). Add a README note that users drop their own JSON packs in /content and that copyrighted text is their problem, not the app's.
- Packs are imported at build time via import.meta.glob. Also support pasting raw text into a "custom passage" box at runtime.

Core typing loop (this is the part to get right):
- Render the passage as individual character spans. Track a cursor index.
- Correct chars go muted-green, incorrect go red with the typed char shown, untyped stay gray, current char has a blinking caret.
- Handle backspace (allow correcting the last error, configurable), ignore modifier keys, prevent browser scroll on space.
- Timer starts on first keystroke, ends on last character. Compute gross WPM (chars/5 per minute), net WPM, and accuracy as a percentage.
- Live WPM readout updates no more than twice a second so it does not jitter.
- A settings panel: blind mode (hide errors until the end), stop-on-error mode, font size, and passage length cap that splits long passages into chunks.

Results and history:
- On finish, show WPM, accuracy, time, and the five characters you missed most.
- Save every run to localStorage: timestamp, pack, passage id, wpm, accuracy.
- A history page with a line chart of WPM over time (recharts) and a per-character error heatmap rendered as a simple keyboard layout.
- Export history as JSON, import it back.

Explicitly out of scope: multiplayer, leaderboards, user accounts, cloud sync, mobile-native app, any AI generated passages.

Keyboard-first: Enter restarts, Tab+Enter advances to next passage, Escape returns to the pack list. No secrets, so no .env needed; if you add any later, read them from .env and commit .env.example only.
